opus-5.5.text:
I think data scaling is probably the single most important lever right now, but I'd frame it a bit differently from how people usually talk about it.

In language models, we had the whole internet as a pre-existing corpus. For embodied intelligence there's no equivalent. Every trajectory has to be collected, by teleoperation, by real robots running in the world, or through simulation. So the question isn't just "do we have enough data?" It's "what kind of data actually transfers, and how do we produce it at a cost that makes scaling possible?"

For embodiment-specific models, the tension is real. If you train only on data from one robot, one gripper, one camera setup, the model can get very good at that body, but you hit a ceiling fast. The amount you can collect on a single platform is limited. On the other hand, if you mix data from many embodiments naively, you get distribution mismatch: different action spaces, kinematics, and control frequencies. So I see it as a layered approach. You want a large, diverse foundation that learns general things about the physical world: how objects move, what contact looks like, what a task means semantically. Then you have a thinner, embodiment-specific layer that maps that understanding onto a particular body's actions. The embodiment-specific data doesn't need to be enormous, but it needs to be high quality and cover the failure modes.

This is also why I'm optimistic about world models and generative approaches. If a model can learn physical dynamics from video, which we have far more of than robot data, it can amplify the value of each real robot trajectory. Simulation and synthetic data play a similar role, as long as we're honest about the sim-to-real gap.

So yes, scaling matters enormously. But blindly scaling one robot's data isn't the answer. The real progress comes from designing a data pyramid where cheap, abundant data teaches general physical common sense and expensive, embodiment-specific data teaches precise control. Getting that ratio and that interface right is, to me, one of the most important open problems in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says an embodiment-specific layer needs data from the particular body to map general understanding to its actions, and that this data must cover failure modes and teach precise control. That conveys the need for sufficient embodiment-specific data to build the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say scaling data is important, but for embodiment-specific models it's a more subtle question than it is in language or vision.

In language, the data was already there. The internet gave us trillions of tokens, and the main work was building models that could absorb it. In embodied intelligence, the data doesn't exist yet in that form. Every robot has its own body, its own sensors, its own action space. A trajectory collected on one arm doesn't transfer cleanly to another. So when people say "just scale the data," the first question is: which data, and for which body?

My view is that there are really two layers. One is the general layer, which is understanding the physical world: how objects move, how things deform, what happens when you push or pour or stack. That layer benefits enormously from scale, and a lot of it can come from video, from simulation, from world models that generate plausible physical outcomes. You don't need a specific robot to learn that a cup falls when you tip it.

The other layer is embodiment-specific: the mapping from that understanding to the actual motor commands of a particular machine. Here scale matters too, but the bottleneck is different. Real robot data is expensive, slow, and often low quality. Collecting ten times more teleoperation data gives you diminishing returns if the diversity doesn't grow with it. So I'd rather see data scaled along the diversity axis, more scenes, more tasks, more failure cases, than simply more hours of the same manipulation.

What I find most promising is using generative models as a bridge. If a world model can simulate the consequences of actions with reasonable fidelity, you can generate embodiment-specific data at scale, and the real robot data becomes the calibration set rather than the entire training set. That flips the economics. Instead of collecting everything physically, you collect enough to ground the model and let synthesis handle the long tail.

So yes, scaling data matters. But for embodied models I think the right framing is scaling the right kind of data, and building the pipeline that makes scaling cheap in the first place. Whoever solves that pipeline problem will have a bigger advantage than whoever simply has the most robots in a warehouse.

r001.rationale: The response argues that embodiment-specific models need data suited to each robot’s body and action space, and that this data must be scaled—through diverse real-world data and synthesized data—to build the model.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling data is essential, but for embodiment-specific models, the question is what you’re scaling. A robot’s observations and actions depend on its body—its sensors, its joints, its gripper. So collecting more data on one embodiment can improve performance on that platform, but it doesn’t automatically translate to another robot.

That’s why I’d look at both quantity and diversity: different tasks, environments, objects, and especially examples of recovering from mistakes. Repeating the same successful motion many times gives you less coverage than those variations.

The interesting challenge is how much knowledge we can share across embodiments, and how much data we still need for each particular body. Ideally, shared data teaches general skills, while embodiment-specific data grounds those skills in what the robot can actually perceive and do.

r001.rationale: The response says embodiment-specific data is needed to ground skills for each robot body, but it does not argue that expecting embodied AI to have its own dedicated model entails collecting enough data to build that model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling data is essential, but for embodiment-specific models, the key question is what we’re scaling. More trajectories on the same robot doing the same task can improve reliability, but that doesn’t necessarily give you generalization. You also need diversity in tasks, environments, objects, and interactions.

Embodiment adds another challenge because the data is tied to a particular body—its sensors, action space, and physical capabilities. If every new robot requires collecting a huge dataset from scratch, that becomes a bottleneck. So I think we need both: enough data from the target embodiment to learn precise control, and ways to share knowledge across embodiments so we don’t have to relearn everything.

Ultimately, I would measure scaling by how much it improves success on unfamiliar tasks and how much less data you need to adapt to a new robot. Those are more meaningful than dataset size alone.

r001.rationale: The response says embodiment-specific models need enough data from the target embodiment to learn precise control, directly conveying that a dedicated embodied model requires sufficient embodiment-specific data.
